claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles is governed by their degree of atomic-scale elemental homogeneity.
Rapid thermal treatment kinetically freezes a uniform elemental distribution.
A rapidly established uniform distribution delays phase segregation relative to conventional slow heating.
A rapidly established uniform distribution delays oxidation relative to conventional slow heating.
Rapid high-temperature synthesis can produce homogeneous, near-equiatomic multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles.
A controlled comparison of rapid and slow thermal ramps, followed by identical service exposure and in situ characterization, can isolate the effect of heating rate.
The relevant catalytic service-temperature range is 773–1173 K.
The relevant thermoelectric service-temperature range is 473–1923 K.
A uniform elemental distribution minimizes local compositional fluctuations.
Minimizing local compositional fluctuations prevents nucleation of reaction-prone sites.
Rapid thermal processing limits atomic diffusion and phase separation during synthesis.
Limiting diffusion and phase separation kinetically hinders formation of intermetallic compounds and oxidized phases.
Slow heating permits diffusion-driven segregation and local oxidation that degrade performance.
Rapidly synthesized nanoparticles will show less elemental segregation and fewer secondary phases than slowly heated controls.
Rapidly synthesized nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance than slowly heated controls.
Rapidly synthesized nanoparticles will have better thermoelectric performance than slowly heated controls.
Conventionally slow-heated nanoparticles are expected to show earlier segregation, phase separation, or surface oxidation under identical service conditions.
The proposed mechanism is most applicable to near-equiatomic multi-element systems with low noble-metal content.
Large differences in elemental diffusivity or substantial deviations from equiatomic composition may weaken the proposed mechanism.
The critical heating rate and its dependence on elemental identity and processing time are not yet quantified.
